documents.title: Mitochondrial Medicine Society consensus recommendations for mitochondrial disease patient care

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT) is a group of inherited neuropathies characterized by progressive length‐dependent limb weakness and sensory deficits. It is estimated to affect 1 in 1 214 to 3 344 individuals [ , ]. CMT is traditionally categorized according to neurophysiologic findings and its mode of inheritance. Demyelinating subtypes of CMT (CMT types 1 and 4) are more common than axonal subtypes (CMT type 2), with CMT1A being the most common subtype overall, affecting up to 50% of all individuals with CMT [ , ]. Currently there are no approved disease modifying therapies for CMT. Many affected individuals are known to develop orthopedic sequelae such as foot deformity, scoliosis, and hip dysplasia [ , , ]. CMT‐associated hip dysplasia typically involves a shallow acetabulum and increased femoral anteversion, along with progressive weakness of both hip abductor and extensor muscles, resulting in altered hip development due to abnormal biomechanics [ ]. The clinical presentation can be variable, ranging from asymptomatic, to joint subluxation or dislocation, which can cause pain, gait impairment, and early joint degeneration. The exact prevalence of hip dysplasia in CMT is unclear. To date, there is only one published series, which estimated the hip dysplasia prevalence between 6%–8.1% [ ]. In that historical cohort, many cases of hip dysplasia were detected from radiographs performed for scoliosis surveillance rather than dedicated pelvic radiographs. Recent clinical practice guidelines for the management of pediatric CMT highlighted the importance of radiologic screening for hip dysplasia; however, consensus was not reached regarding the timing or frequency of radiologic surveillance [ ]. The evolution of the risk of hip dysplasia in CMT during childhood in those with normal initial pelvic radiographs or minor abnormalities is unknown, making consensus recommendations regarding the frequency of ongoing radiologic surveillance difficult to achieve. The primary aim of this study was to describe the prevalence of hip dysplasia in children with CMT seen at a large tertiary pediatric neuromuscular center. Secondary aims were to describe the natural history of hip development as indicated by radiographs through skeletal development, and ultimately propose recommended timing and frequency of pelvic radiograph evaluation in children with CMT. 2 Methods and Materials This retrospective study was conducted at the Royal Children's Hospital, Melbourne (RCH) between 1st July 2021 and 31st December 2021. Ethical approval was obtained from RCH Research Ethics & Governance (HREC Reference Number: QA/78576/RCHM‐2021). 2.1 Inclusion Criteria The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) children seen in the neuromuscular clinic at RCH with CMT and/or related disorders, including the hereditary motor neuropathies and hereditary sensory neuropathies, (ii) genetically confirmed CMT and/or a consistent clinical and neurophysiologic phenotype, (iii) at least one pelvic radiograph performed between 2000 and 2020 which was available for review, and (iv) less than 18 years of age at the time of the first pelvic radiograph. Children who did not have pelvic radiography performed were excluded. Children meeting eligibility criteria were retrieved from the medical files by using the Electronic Medical Record (EPIC) Slicer Dicer function, and cross‐referenced with the RCH neuromuscular clinic database to ensure all eligible children had been identified. 2.2 Clinical Characteristics Demographic data, subtype of CMT, genetic diagnosis, age at identification of hip dysplasia, indication for hip radiography, presence of motor delay, ambulation status, symptoms of hip disease and surgical treatments performed were collected for analysis. Children with gross motor delay included those that did not walk by 18 months of age. Children with a history of developmental hip dysplasia diagnosed with hip ultrasound during infancy were also classified as having clinical symptoms as the indication for initial hip radiography. Hip maturity by radiograph was defined as age 14 years and above for females, and 16 years and above for males [ ]. 2.3 Pelvic Radiographs At the RCH, the historic practice pattern has been for initial pelvic radiography to be arranged at the discretion of the treating neurologist, regardless of the presence of symptoms. This practice has been in place for many years, but it has varied amongst clinicians and over time in terms of the age at first radiograph and the frequency of follow‐up radiography. Some children managed in the early years of the data collection period did not have any pelvic radiographs performed. Additionally, many children with early abnormalities had radiographs variably repeated for subsequent monitoring. Therefore, the number and frequency of pelvic radiographs performed per child varied according to the treating clinician. A senior pediatric orthopedic surgeon (CK) evaluated all pelvic radiographs. For each radiograph Reimer's migration percentage (MP), acetabular index (AI), and lateral center edge angle (LCEA) were measured to ascertain hip and acetabular dysplasia. pelvic radiographs performed. Additionally, many children with early abnormalities had radiographs variably repeated for subsequent monitoring. Therefore, the number and frequency of pelvic radiographs performed per child varied according to the treating clinician. A senior pediatric orthopedic surgeon (CK) evaluated all pelvic radiographs. For each radiograph Reimer's migration percentage (MP), acetabular index (AI), and lateral center edge angle (LCEA) were measured to ascertain hip and acetabular dysplasia. These have been demonstrated to be reliable and sensitive measures of hip dysplasia in children with CMT [ ]. MP quantifies the proportion of the ossified femoral head that lies outside the confines of the bony acetabulum on the anterior–posterior pelvis radiograph, as defined by the percentage of the femoral head width, which is lateral to Perkin's line relative to the entirety of the head width [ , ]. AI measures the shallowness of the acetabulum, and LCEA measures the lateral coverage of the femoral head. AI was defined as the angle formed from a line drawn from the lateral margin of the acetabulum and Hilgenreiner's line, which is drawn connecting the bilateral triradiate cartilage [ ]. Lateral center‐edge angle was defined as a line extending vertically from the femoral head and a line subtending the lateral edge of the acetabulum [ ]. In this study, hip dysplasia was defined radiologically as: (i) MP > 30% at any age [ ], and/or (ii) LCEA < 25° in skeletally mature patients and/or (iii) AI > 25° in a child over 2 years of age. Neck‐shaft angle was not used as a marker to define hip dysplasia given the evidence of inferior reliability compared to other radiographic indices in hip dysplasia in CMT [ ]. 2.4 Statistical Analysis Data was collected using Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) tool hosted on a secure network at the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, Melbourne, and analyzed using Stata SE 17.0 (StataCorp LLC. USA). Demographic data, hip dysplasia, and clinical and radiographic characteristics were summarized descriptively, using median and interquartile range (IQR), and frequency and percentage where appropriate. On advice from a biostatistician, linear and logistic regression analyses were not undertaken for this study due to the limited sample size. 3 Results A total of 256 children with CMT were identified. Seventy‐eight children were excluded, including 77 who had no hip radiographs for review, and one with a complex neurodevelopmental disorder, leaving 178 eligible children (Figure ). Demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table . The median age at diagnosis of CMT was 6.4 years and a male preponderance (58.4%) was noted. CMT subtypes were classified as demyelinating, axonal and intermediate in 65.2%, 26.4% and 8.4% of cases respectively. With regards to specific CMT subtypes, 56.2% of children had CMT1A, followed by 6.2% with CMTX1 and 5.6% with CMT2A (Table ). Seven children had Dejerine‐Sottas disease (DSD), a clinical phenotype associated with an early‐onset demyelinating neuropathy [ , ]. More than half of children (102 children; 57.3%) had normal gross motor development, while 43 (24.2%) had delayed gross motor development. Only 98 children (55.1%) completed a CMT Pediatric Scale (CMTPedS) assessment [ ]; many were seen prior to its development and implementation (Figure ). Children aged less than 10 years tended to have disability of mild to moderate severity as measured by the CMTPedS score, whilst those who were older than 10 years of age had higher levels of disability [ ]. A total of 50 children (28.1%) fulfilled our radiographic criteria of hip dysplasia based on their final radiograph (Figure ). This included 12 children who were retrospectively diagnosed with hip dysplasia with our radiographic criteria after a single hip radiograph but had no further imaging as the hip radiograph was reported to be normal by the radiologist. The median age of the first pelvic radiograph was 8.0 years (IQR 4.6–12.2 years). The majority (58.4%) were screening radiographs, whilst only 9.6% (17 children) of pelvic radiographs were performed based on clinical symptoms or history of dysplasia on infant hip ultrasound (Table ). On their initial pelvic radiograph, 64 children (36.0%) were diagnosed with hip dysplasia (Table ). Of these, 12 (18.8%) required immediate surgical intervention. Based on their first pelvic radiograph, serial pelvic radiography was performed in the remaining 52 children, of which 20 normalized with age. Thirty‐two children had persistent radiographic hip dysplasia, of whom five eventually required hip surgery. Therefore, a total of 17 children required surgical management of hip dysplasia (9.6% of the 178‐patient cohort) (Figure ). Children with DSD had the highest rates of hip dysplasia at first radiograph (6 out of 7 children). Of these children, the median age of diagnosis of DSD and timing of the first radiograph was similar (age 2.3 years). Children with DSD had the highest rates of hip dysplasia at first radiograph (6 out of 7 children). Of these children, the median age of diagnosis of DSD and timing of the first radiograph was similar (age 2.3 years). One child with DSD required immediate surgery at the time of diagnosis of hip dysplasia. Forty‐five children with demyelinating forms of CMT had hip dysplasia at first radiograph, with CMT1A accounting for 82.2% (37/45). The median age of the diagnosis of CMT1A in this cohort was 4.9 years, and the first radiograph was performed at a median age of 5.8 years. Eight children with CMT1A (8/37) required immediate surgical intervention. Hip dysplasia was detected in 18 children with axonal forms of CMT. In this cohort, the median age of diagnosis of CMT and first radiograph were 5.5 and 3.4 years respectively and included six children who had a pelvic radiograph performed prior to the diagnosis of CMT. Three children required surgery (two had TPRV4 ‐related CMT and one had no genetic diagnosis). There were 17 children who had their initial pelvic radiograph performed based on either follow‐up after an abnormal prior infant hip ultrasound (4 children) or clinical symptoms which included a Trendelenburg gait (5 children), abnormal hip range of motion (3 children), proximal lower limb weakness (2 children), hip pain (1 child), “clicky hips” on examination (1 child) and combination of symptoms of hip pain, Trendelenburg gait and abnormal hip range of motion (1 child). Of these 17 children, 11 (64.7%) were diagnosed with hip dysplasia at their first pelvic radiograph and five required surgical intervention. Of these five children, two were diagnosed with hip dysplasia due to hip pain and asymmetric range of movement in the hip respectively, and three (all with axonal forms of CMT) were diagnosed with developmental dysplasia of the hip on ultrasound during infancy. In comparison, 31/104 (29.8%) of those who had pelvic radiographs as part of anticipatory screening had radiographic hip dysplasia; four of whom required surgical intervention. The reason for the initial radiograph was unclear in 57 children, of whom 22 (38.6%) had radiographic hip dysplasia. Therefore, only 11/42 (26.2%) children with available data regarding the indication for their initial pelvic radiograph were symptomatic at the time of diagnosis of hip dysplasia. In 114 children who had normal first pelvic radiographs, six developed hip dysplasia on subsequent radiographs (Figure ), but none required surgical intervention. In these six children, the initial radiographs were performed at a young age (1.2–4 years) and the interval between the first normal radiograph and subsequent diagnosis of hip dysplasia ranged between 1 and 8.3 years (Figure ). Eight children were non‐ambulant at the time the study was performed (Figure ). Three never achieved independent walking—one with TRPV4‐ related CMT, one with MPZ ‐related DSD and one with axonal CMT and no genetic diagnosis (Figure ). Another three used walking aides prior to loss of ambulation. Six out of these eight children were diagnosed with hip dysplasia on their first pelvic radiograph. Of these six children, five had hip dysplasia at last follow up, four of whom required surgical intervention. In one, the pelvic radiograph normalized over the time. At the time of last follow up, 28.1% (50/178) of the whole cohort had hip dysplasia, which included 28% (28/100) of children with CMT1A, 5/7 with DSD, 3/10 with CMT2A and 4/4 with TRPV4 ‐related phenotypes (Figure ). Surgical correction was required in 17/178 (9.6%) of the whole cohort. Nine out of 28 (32.1%) children with CMT1A and hip dysplasia underwent hip surgery, whilst three out of five children with DSD and hip dysplasia needed surgery. The remaining five children who required surgical intervention included children with pathogenic variants in TRPV4 and BICD2 . 4 Discussion In this single center cohort of children with CMT, 36.0% (64/178) children were diagnosed with hip dysplasia on their first pelvic radiograph, and 28.1% (50/178) had hip dysplasia at last follow up. This included 12 children who were diagnosed with hip dysplasia after a single pelvic radiograph with no further imaging follow up. We are uncertain how many of these 12 children had persistent hip dysplasia or resolved their hip under‐development with age. This included 12 children who were diagnosed with hip dysplasia after a single pelvic radiograph with no further imaging follow up. We are uncertain how many of these 12 children had persistent hip dysplasia or resolved their hip under‐development with age. If we were to exclude these 12 children, this would leave 38/166 (22.9%) with confirmed hip dysplasia on serial imaging. Hip dysplasia was often asymptomatic in this cohort. Given that 17 (9.6%) children had severe enough pathology to require surgical intervention, we estimate that the true prevalence of hip dysplasia in children with CMT and related disorders may be between 9.6% and 22.9%. This prevalence is higher than the historical cohort reported by Walker et al. at 6%–8.1% [ ]. This could be explained by several reasons. Firstly, our center has adopted active screening of hip dysplasia for many years due to an awareness of the association between CMT and hip dysplasia. Secondly, the criteria used by Walker et al. to diagnose hip dysplasia were more stringent compared to our study as it required three abnormal radiographic parameters. If we applied the similar radiographic criteria used by Walker et al. in our cohort, the prevalence in our cohort ranged between 9.6%–14.6% (Table ), with the upper limit higher than the rate reported by Walker et al. Thirdly, the majority of our cohort involved children who were skeletally immature. We believe that some of the younger children identified with hip dysplasia reflect developmental hip immaturity, which may normalize over time. Children with CMT1A, of whom nearly 10% required surgical intervention before adolescence, formed the largest group of children with hip dysplasia. This is unsurprising given this is the most common type of CMT. In comparison, despite children with CMT2A having comparable rates of radiographic hip dysplasia (30%), these were mild cases and none required surgical intervention. This is discordant with the greater clinical severity of CMT2A compared to CMT1A [ ]. Dysplasia was also less common in children with CMTX type 1 (10%, with none requiring surgery). The reason for these differences, and the apparent predilection for hip dysplasia in demyelinating forms of CMT is unclear, but it was also noted in the Walker study that all children with definite hip dysplasia had CMT type 1 [ ]. The small numbers of the less common CMT subtypes in this genetically heterogeneous cohort mean this finding needs to be replicated in larger cohorts. However, even with small numbers, disproportionately higher rates of radiographic hip dysplasia were seen in children with Dejerine‐Sottas disease (71.4%) and children with TRPV4 ‐related axonal CMT (100%), with a high rate of surgery. Many of these children were also non ambulant, indicating that ambulation status is likely an independent risk factor of hip dysplasia in children with CMT. The association of bone dysplasia with TRPV4 mutations may also be a factor contributing to hip dysplasia in this specific CMT subtype [ ]. Six children who had a normal first hip radiograph at an early age later developed hip dysplasia. None of these children needed surgical intervention. Five of these children had CMT1A and the initial radiographs were done at the age of 4 years or younger. As such, it is our view that a radiograph prior to 4 years of age does not definitively rule out hip dysplasia in patients with CMT1A. We advocate for a radiograph being repeated at a later age, even in the absence of symptoms or physical exam findings. No children with CMT1A were diagnosed with hip dysplasia after the age of 10.5 years in our cohort. We suspect that dysplasia was likely to have been diagnosed prior to that age, but did not have interval radiographs to evaluate this. The clinical practice guideline for pediatric CMT states that a hip radiograph should be considered in all children to screen for hip dysplasia [ ]. The findings from this study support this recommendation. We additionally recommend that children should have their first pelvic radiograph performed soon after the diagnosis of CMT is made, particularly if one has not been performed prior. Secondly, we recommend that in the absence of symptoms of hip dysplasia, a follow up screening radiograph is performed at an interval of every 2 to 3 years in ambulant children and that ongoing radiographic monitoring is generally not required after 14 years of age for females and 16 years of age for males by which time skeletal maturity is imminent. In non‐ambulant children with CMT, or children with DSD or mutations in TRPV4 , more frequent clinical and/or radiographic monitoring of hips should be considered, particularly if there are no documented radiographic improvements on prior radiographs. of every 2 to 3 years in ambulant children and that ongoing radiographic monitoring is generally not required after 14 years of age for females and 16 years of age for males by which time skeletal maturity is imminent. In non‐ambulant children with CMT, or children with DSD or mutations in TRPV4 , more frequent clinical and/or radiographic monitoring of hips should be considered, particularly if there are no documented radiographic improvements on prior radiographs. This study of hip dysplasia in 178 CMT children is the largest in the published literature. Walker et al. original study involved 74 children who had pelvis radiographs and pre‐dated the era of genetic diagnosis. Our study includes a confirmed genetic diagnosis in 149/178 (83.7%) of our cohort, thus providing additional information regarding prevalence and severity of dysplasia according to genetic diagnosis. The management of hip dysplasia in the adolescent population has changed dramatically in the last 20 years. Historically, native hip reconstructive options for adolescent and adult patients were quite limited; most reconstructions involving the acetabular side of the hip were offered in early childhood, otherwise the patient was left with their own hip until the point of sufficient degeneration and pain occurred, and then they would be offered a total hip replacement. The Periacetabular Osteotomy (PAO), developed by Ganz et al. [ ], has become the procedure of choice over the past 15 years to treat hip dysplasia in skeletally mature patients [ , ], and is done with the goal of alleviating symptoms and preserving a native hip, thereby avoiding or delaying degeneration and joint replacement. Thus, in the current era, there is an imperative to identify cases of hip dysplasia in the pediatric and adolescent age group, well before the hip degenerates. Based on these factors, we believe that the radiographic criteria for hip dysplasia used in the Walker et al. [ ] study may not be adequately sensitive in the current era, given the reconstructive options available. We acknowledge several limitations of this study. Firstly, our study is retrospective and the number of patients with rarer forms of CMT is limited. Data was not available for all patients and the lack of a prospective cohort design mean that potential risk factors, such as the presence of hip abductor weakness could not be adequately analyzed. Secondly, during this period there were no clear recommendations about the timing of hip surveillance. As such, the acquisition of pelvic radiographs was based on individual clinician discretion and awareness of hip dysplasia risk. Thirdly, the indication for performing hip radiographs was not well documented and standardized in this cohort. Lastly, we also noticed, in retrospect, that there were some inconsistent findings between radiologists and orthopedic clinicians in recognition of the diagnosis of radiographic hip dysplasia. This was the case especially with “minor abnormalities,” in which radiographs were initially reported as “normal” and, hence, no further surveillance radiographs were arranged, leading to a potential under‐recognition of hip dysplasia in this group of children who are mainly managed by neurology specialists. This study confirms a significant association between hip dysplasia and childhood onset CMT and validates the current recommendation for radiographic hip surveillance in children with CMT [ ]. We hope that a large prospective study can be carried out in the future to delineate the natural history of hip development, risk factors for, and the underlying biomechanics causing the development of hip dysplasia, and inform more detailed evidence‐based recommendations for the surveillance and management of hip dysplasia in children with CMT.
